summary.text: A 3-year-old boy presented with abdominal distension and constipation, described as persisting for several months and elsewhere for his entire life, with intermittent blackish stool, a delay in stool passage in the first 4 days of life and blood in the stool that prompted an initial CMPA diagnosis treated conservatively with laxatives.

Examination showed a soft, significantly distended abdomen with mild soiling and anatomically normal anal examination. Blood count, tissue transglutaminase IgA and thyroid function were normal. Abdominal X-ray and contrast CT showed dilated bowel loops and a distended colon, and barium enema was planned for suspected Hirschsprung disease.

Rectal biopsy showed focal absence of ganglion cells over about 3 cm of distal bowel and Hirschsprung disease was diagnosed. Laparoscopic colostomy was performed for acute symptoms, followed 2 months later by laparoscopic pull-through proctectomy and then colostomy reversal. Recovery was uneventful and he remained well and symptom-free at follow-up visits.

summary.text: A 2-month-old girl presented with regular greenish-yellow vomiting, good oral intake and normal regular bowel movements, with no significant medical or family history. Normal barium studies at another facility were followed by a CMPA diagnosis and an exclusion diet without improvement; the authors call the CMPA/gastroesophageal regurgitation diagnosis a misdiagnosis.

Examination showed an obviously distended gassy abdomen with mild perianal erythema, normal anal position and an otherwise unremarkable examination; no laboratory testing was conducted. Barium swallow showed an abnormally positioned duodenal jejunal junction with small bowel loops on the right, and chest X-ray incidentally showed bifid vertebrae; partial malrotation/incomplete rotation was diagnosed.

She underwent laparoscopic Ladd’s procedure with resection of Ladd’s bands, appendectomy and umbilical hernia repair, had an uneventful postoperative period, good weight gain and complete resolution of symptoms throughout follow-up visits.

summary.text: A 6-month-old boy presented with persistent vomiting and severe failure to thrive; he had good weight gain from birth until 3 months, then frequent non-bilious vomiting progressing to vomiting after each feeding, without diarrhea, jaundice, abdominal swelling, perianal rash or recurrent infections. He was born at term at 3.2 kg, weight had dropped below the 0.4 percentile, and a previous CMPA diagnosis with a cow’s milk protein-free formula did not improve symptoms.

He was dehydrated and significantly malnourished with reduced subcutaneous fat and muscle bulk, an unusual cry with stridor, anxious look and irritability; baseline, renal, liver, immunoglobulin and thyroid tests were normal. Ultrasound showed gallbladder sludge/stone and prominent pylorus muscles; barium swallow showed a markedly dilated thoracic esophagus with a bird beak sign and persistent contrast pooling, and achalasia was diagnosed.

He was admitted for rehydration, monitoring and workup, started on an amino acid formula, had chest and abdominal CT and then laparoscopic Heller myotomy, a brief uneventful postoperative stay and an overall outstanding outcome with full feeds and excellent weight gain at follow-up.
